To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) bilinguals and monolinquals alike exhibit robust correlations between mixing cost and switching cost across tasks and across CTIs, but (2) only bilinguals show significantly smaller task-switch costs than monolinquals at a long CTI, and this effect is diminished with practice, and (3) practice effects in switching costs are larger at a short CTI.

1) bilingualism was associated with reduced task-switching costs, but only with long preparation time (i.e., long cue–target intervals), and only in the first 20 trials, 2) bilinguals committed fewer task-switching errors, especially at short preparation time, but 3) mixing costs were not associated with bilingualism or preparation time, and 4) task-switching costs were not associated between tasks (color-shape vs. language-switching), whereas mixing costs
bilinguals exhibited smaller task switching costs than monolingals when the cue-target interval was long, and this difference was observed only in the first block of trials.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how bilingualism affects the ability to switch between tasks.
the association between language switching and task switching.
the association between bilingualism, switching efficiency, and general switching ability, and the role of practice effects and task specificity in this relation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are some indications of an advantage for bilinguals, but it may be limited to specific task manipulations and contexts.
bilinguals may have a relative advantage in switching, but this advantage depends on task manipulations, practice, and cognitive mechanisms.
bilingualism is not associated with general switching efficiency, and that the evidence for such an association is mixed and may depend on experimental manipulations that are not well understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
bilinguals are better at task switching than monolingual speakers, but the effects are more complex than previously thought.

bilinguals may be more efficient switchers, especially when switching requires preparation, but that these differences are likely to be small and may be obscured in studies with short cue–target intervals and few practice trials.
bilingualism is related to switching efficiency, especially when the ability to switch is more generally taxed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
bilingualism is not a panacea for switching deficits, but may be a protective factor for switching efficiency in the face of cognitive aging.
the association between bilingualism, switching and executive control is nuanced, and that more work is needed to understand the mechanisms underlying this relationship.
bilinguals are not necessarily superior at switching, but may have a relative advantage when switching is made more difficult.
